purpose: Oxaliplatin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat colon and rectal cancer. It is often given together with other chemotherapy drugs to help fight cancer that has spread or to lower the chance of cancer coming back after surgery. Your cancer care team will use it as part of a carefully planned treatment program.
how_it_works: Oxaliplatin works by attaching itself to the DNA inside cancer cells, which is like the instruction manual that tells cells how to grow and divide. When the DNA gets damaged this way, the cancer cells can no longer copy themselves properly and they die off. Because it targets fast-growing cells, it is very effective against cancer, though it can also affect some healthy cells in your body.
common_side_effects: Very common side effects include numbness, tingling, or unusual sensitivity to cold in your hands, feet, and mouth — this is called neuropathy and is the most well-known side effect of this drug. You may also experience nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, and low blood cell counts which can make you more prone to infections or bruising. Mouth sores and loss of appetite are also frequently reported.
warnings: The cold sensitivity can be serious — avoid touching cold objects or drinking cold liquids right after your infusion, as it can cause painful or unusual sensations. Oxaliplatin can cause serious allergic reactions during or shortly after the infusion, so tell your nurse immediately if you feel flushed, have trouble breathing, or feel dizzy. Long-term nerve damage in the hands and feet is possible, so always report new or worsening numbness or tingling to your doctor. This drug can also lower your blood counts, increasing your risk of infections, bleeding, and anemia.
typical_dosing: Oxaliplatin is given through an IV (intravenous infusion) in a clinic or hospital — you cannot take it as a pill at home. The infusion usually lasts about 2 hours and is typically given once every 2 weeks as part of a chemotherapy combination regimen. Your exact dose is carefully calculated based on your body size and overall health, and your oncology team will monitor you closely throughout your treatment.
